We should quote the following passage because it clearly shows Ibn Sīnā’s method in his theory of universals. He says: “Universals, and the judgments and concepts that concern them, are not grasped by the senses or imagination, nor are they themselves objects of intuition or experience. But the senses and imagination assist the intellect. As for forming concepts: the senses present mixed things to the imagination, the imagination presents them to the intellect, and the intellect then separates, distinguishes, and divides them. It takes each meaning on its own and arranges what is more particular and more general, what belongs to the essence and what is accidental. In this way the first meanings needed for concepts become present in the intellect, and it then combines them into definitions. As for judgments, the senses and imagination may assist [the intellect] through experience or intuition, and they may assist it through induction.... They may also assist indirectly: first by helping to supply the concepts, after which the concepts are combined through affirmation and negation. The intellect then sees what must be accepted as self-evident, and it sees the syllogism by which other judgments must be acquired.” The Salvation, pp. 65–66. This passage gives a detailed account of how the intellect moves from sensory experience to the universal. It confirms that, in Ibn Sīnā’s theory of universals, the intellect depends on sensory experience. Intuition is mentioned here only incidentally. We will return to this later.↩︎

Modern scholars disagree about the intellectual relationship between Pointers and Reminders and Ibn Sīnā’s earlier works, especially The Healing and The Salvation. Some argue that when Ibn Sīnā wrote Pointers and Reminders, as well as his symbolic stories—The Treatise of the Bird, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Salāmān and Absāl, and The Treatise on Love—he moved away from the Peripatetic ideas that stand out in The Healing and finally turned toward a Sufi form of illuminationist wisdom. This view is represented, for example, by L. Gardet in his article on the religious idea in Ibn Sīnā, published in Revue du Caire, June 1951, and by Sulaymān Dunyā in the introduction to his Cairo 1947 edition of Pointers and Reminders. Other scholars deny that The Healing and Ibn Sīnā’s other early works ceased to express his real views. This is the position of scholars such as Carra de Vaux, Avicenna, Arabic ed., p. 150, and the French Orientalist A. M. Goichon in The Philosophy of Ibn Sīnā, Arabic ed., Beirut, 1950, p. 18. We accept this second view. We have found nothing in Pointers and Reminders that Ibn Sīnā had not already said in his other works. The book differs mainly in two ways. The first is formal: the way it is composed, the material is arranged, and the discussion is divided into sections. The second concerns expression: the style used to present the ideas and the beauty of the language. The writing is more concentrated and compressed, and in the later chapters Ibn Sīnā sometimes uses symbols and sometimes interprets the outward wording of Qurʾānic passages. These stylistic features may be what idealist scholars used to support the claim that Ibn Sīnā changed the positions expressed in his earlier works, where some materialist tendencies are visible, and ended by adopting an illuminationist-Sufi outlook. Some of these scholars also appeal to remarks in the introduction to a work published under Ibn Sīnā’s name as The Logic of the Easterners (Cairo, 1910), where he appears to

under Ibn Sīnā’s name as The Logic of the Easterners (Cairo, 1910), where he appears to disagree with the Peripatetics. They also use Ibn Ṭufayl’s statement in the introduction to Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān that Ibn Sīnā said at the beginning of The Healing that the truth as he understood it was different from what that book contained. See Ibn Ṭufayl, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Dār al-Maʿārif ed., Beirut, 1954, p. 8. In reality, even in The Healing, Ibn Sīnā does not agree completely with Aristotle or with Peripatetic philosophy in general. He differs from them on many points and alters many positions. As for the special section of Pointers and Reminders on the “Stations of the Knowers,” first, it is a mixture of ideas scattered through his other books; and second, it is a descriptive discussion, not a reflection of Ibn Sīnā’s own way of life, as we know from his historically well-established biography.↩︎

The Qurʾānic passage in question is: “God is the light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is as a niche containing a lamp; the lamp is in a glass; the glass is like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it—light upon light...” (Qurʾān 24:35). Ibn Sīnā applies this verse to the levels of intellect in his own theory. He interprets the “niche” as the material intellect; the “olive tree” as the thinking faculty—that is, rational reflection assisted by sensory perceptions; the “oil” as intuition, through which knowledge is gained without discursive thought; the “glass” as the habitual intellect; the phrase “whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it” as the highest degree of intuition, which he calls the holy faculty; and “light upon light” as the stage of perfection reached when the intellect becomes an acquired intellect. He interprets the “lamp” as the rational faculty once it becomes an actual intellect: the human soul can then “bring before itself, whenever it wishes, an intelligible already acquired and completed as though it were directly present, without needing to acquire it again” (Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, pp. 369–376). Al-Ghazālī, however, reverses the relation and treats the Qurʾānic verse as an interpretation of these levels of theoretical intellect. See al-Ghazālī, The Niche of Lights, p. 58.↩︎

In logic, the middle term is the universal proposition relied on in a syllogism to move from what is known to what is unknown—that is, from the minor premise to the required conclusion. This universal proposition, which functions as the middle term, may come either from first rational principles, or axioms, or from theoretical propositions derived from the particulars of external reality. In both cases, even for Ibn Sīnā himself, it is a reflection of external reality, as we concluded earlier from his theory of how first principles are known.↩︎

The question of how consciousness arises in the brain remained unclear to scientists until the famous Soviet scientist Pavlov explained it in the way we described earlier. Before Marx, this question remained a puzzle even for materialist philosophers. Like the idealists, some materialists would say either that consciousness is an essence completely independent of matter, so that body and consciousness work separately but in parallel by some kind of miracle, or they would give a crude explanation and say that the brain secretes thought just as the mouth secretes saliva—that thought simply flows from it automatically. Lenin criticized this crude view, arguing that explaining thought as matter is just as false as explaining matter as thought, because vulgar materialism quickly slips into idealism.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā wrote a special chapter in The Salvation (p. 189) entitled “On the Unity of the Soul,” where he argues that the soul is a single entity in which all the faculties of the soul come together. From this he reaches an important conclusion: he acknowledges that the existence of the soul and the existence of the body are one. Yet he finally maintains that the soul does not arise from a body, “but from a substance whose substantiality is separate” (p. 192). This confirms what we have said: he saw the appearance of unity without seeing the underlying reality of that unity.↩︎

One might object that this statement, the one before it, and the earlier examples we cited of the intellect forming universals from particulars—as in the case of an eclipse—occur in Ibn Sīnā’s discussion of divine matters, or metaphysics, and therefore do not apply to the material world. Our answer is twofold. First, Ibn Sīnā uses ideas of this kind in that context because he treats them as general principles already accepted in the particular sciences, such as natural science and mathematics. He then uses them as grounds for his views in “divine science.” Second, we do not separate a philosopher’s ideas in metaphysics from his ideas in other fields. All of them come from a single source: the real world reflected in his thought in one form or another. His metaphysical ideas are simply one form of that reflection. They are particular echoes of the way he relates to the real world and of his particular position in society.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā often describes the individuating features of a particular thing as “accidents” or “concomitants” that are foreign to its essence—meaning its substance and true nature. We should not take this to mean that he imagines the substance of a thing as a spiritual substance to which matter is attached only accidentally or by chance. That idea is far from his thought. Although he calls these material individuating features “accidents” or “concomitants,” he still regards them as necessarily bound up with the existence of things and impossible to separate from them. We will clarify this point further when we study the theory of form and matter in Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy.↩︎

Aristotle sees the relation of matter to form as similar to the relation of the individual to the universal that includes it and other individuals. Form, in other words, is the concept or essence in relation to matter. Callias and Socrates, Aristotle’s example, are the same in species but differ from one another in their matter (Aristotle, Metaphysics, 7, 1034a 5 ff.). Ibn Sīnā, by contrast, treats matter as the underlying “subject” in relation to form, and this subject is a substance. “Subject” and “substance” are not the same as essence. See The Salvation, p. 200; and al-Shahrastānī, Religions and Sects, vol. 2, p. 74. We will explain this point in detail in the discussion that follows.↩︎

In defining the subject of natural science, Ibn Sīnā says that it is “existing bodies insofar as they undergo change and insofar as they are described by different kinds of motion and rest” (The Salvation, p. 98).↩︎

Aristotle’s dualism of matter and form appears in two ways. First, he treats matter as merely receptive and passive, while form alone is active and acts upon matter. He does not recognize the dialectical unity of mutual influence between them in the way Ibn Sīnā does. See Aristotle, Metaphysics, 7, 1029a 19. Second, matter itself has a double character in Aristotle’s view. Matter is potentiality in relation to form, while form is the actual realization of that potentiality. Matter is therefore pure possibility on one side, and an actual reality realized through form on the other. In this sense it becomes relative: a thing is matter—that is, existence—from one point of view, and form—that is, concept—from another. Matter in itself is therefore not treated as something definite in relation to form. See Aristotle, same source, 7, 1041a–b 5–6. We will see in the course of the discussion how Ibn Sīnā overcame this problem partly, if not completely.↩︎

In ancient and then medieval philosophy, the term “divine science” meant philosophy of existence in its broadest sense—universal being as a whole. It was the main branch of ancient philosophy, which is why Aristotle called it “first philosophy.” Philosophy at that time included all the sciences and was even called “the science of sciences.” Sciences that dealt with particular kinds of existence, such as natural science, mathematics, and social science, were called particular sciences. For this reason, when Ibn Sīnā speaks of “divine science” in this older sense, we treat him as speaking about philosophy, and we treat the principles of that science as the principles of philosophy itself.↩︎

Alongside the many examples already mentioned and others that will appear later, we can give one concrete example here. It occurs in The Salvation (pp. 236–237) in the proof of the Necessary Existent, within the “divine” section of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy. In arguing that “there must be something that necessarily exists,” Ibn Sīnā uses a proof by division in the Platonic manner. When his divisions of possible existence reach the possibility of something coming into being and then ceasing to exist immediately, with no interval of time—in other words, coming to be and passing away at the same instant—he says this is impossible “because instants do not follow one another [as discrete units], and for numerically distinct individuals to come into existence one after another without the continuity found in something like motion would require instants [times] to follow one another, and natural science has already shown this to be impossible....” Ibn Sīnā is therefore using a law of natural science as part of a proof in “divine science.” This is a concrete example of how he relies on theoretical generalizations drawn from the study of nature in arguments concerning the metaphysical world.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā does not picture the “first mover” as motionless in the way Aristotle does. He speaks clearly and explicitly on this point: “A mover implies something moved. But this implication does not mean that the moved thing must be something other than the mover, or that it must be the mover itself. (...) We therefore did not rule out the possibility of conceiving something that moves itself until a proof establishes that this is impossible. The mere concepts of mover and moved do not themselves rule it out. A moved thing requires something from which its motion comes, without requiring that this be either another thing or itself; and a mover requires something moved by it, without requiring that this be either another thing or itself....” The Salvation, p. 244.↩︎

Elsewhere in Pointers and Reminders (vol. 3, pp. 88–89), Ibn Sīnā also explains that terms such as “acted,” “made,” and “brought into existence” are used when something was first non-existent and then comes into existence after non-existence because of some cause. We then call it an effect, or something produced. An eternal existent, therefore, is not called an effect because, as he says in the passage quoted above, “non-existence did not precede it.” This confirms that Ibn Sīnā deliberately rejects the relation of acting, agency, and being acted upon between the first cause and its effect, the world, because this effect is as eternal as its cause.↩︎
